title: I Used the Hurdy-Gurdy Crank Log on the Mentor Who Left My Numbered Cotton

parts.text: I stepped into the wheel room at 3:06 p.m. and mentor Brigid was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE WHEEL. SIXTY MINUTES. COTTON STAYS WITH THE SLOT. I was thirty-three, studio secretary, holding a checkout that listed our numbered cotton. Brigid shrugged. "Mentors are the crank." I photographed the board, the booking, and her leftover rosin on my numbered cotton. Then I asked for the crank log. At 3:14 the desk pinged why Brigid's name was on my wheel. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The desk can see Brigid's leftover rosin on my numbered cotton.

social.video_title: She left my numbered hurdy-gurdy cotton on my wheel — Part 1/2
social.description: Wheel room, leftover rosin, a sixty-minute clock she posted. I logged the crank. Would you have asked for the crank log?

parts.text: Brigid called it cotton dressing until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the rosin still. The cotton went back to my numbered slot. Brigid ran a slot of her own and told the next mentor atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: MENTORS ARE NOT THE CRANK. I keep my cotton in a labeled tin. Brigid brown-bags her dressing. The wheel room finally looks like a slot, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Mentors are not the crank — Part 2/2
social.description: Crank log, numbered cotton, and a second line on the board. Was cotton dressing ever my wheel?
